analysis.title: Cracks In The AI Boom?
key_insights: Perkins argues AI ecosystem revenues are still mostly capex recycling (hyperscaler spending flowing back as revenue within the ecosystem), not demand from outside businesses and end-users, which he says is not a mark of genuine sustainability.

Studies published since June put the hurdle rate (revenue needed for an adequate return on capital) on AI revenue at $2.5-3.5 trillion a year by 2030. Enterprise revenue is about $200bn today, so the gap is large.
The AI revenue needed would require consumers to spend as much on AI services as they do on food, which Perkins calls unlikely.

AI financing leverage is rising quickly. The weak points are debt at unprofitable neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers and equipment/power providers, not the hyperscalers, whose balance sheets he calls pristine. He notes hyperscalers might not renew all rolling datacenter leases.

AI-related debt could reach $2 trillion by end-2027. Perkins says it is not a systemic issue but could become a problem if earnings disappoint and misses cascade through the ecosystem as cancelled orders.

Tech hardware and chips are cyclical and prone to bullwhip effects. Perkins cites reports of companies double- and triple-ordering chips in anticipation of shortages, so a demand slowdown could turn shortages into a glut. He also flags NVIDIA's vendor financing.

Some analysts warn of 'teaser rate' effects, as in subprime. Perkins calls the comparison stretched but says accounting practices flatter AI balance sheets, including the 'depreciation cliff' that appears only after data centers are completed, and data center leases.
In the teaser period the seller reports backlogs while the buyer, a cash-burning frontier lab, books no expense because the capacity does not yet exist.

The trigger for a bust need not come from inside the boom. Perkins names rate hikes and politics as candidates, arguing ordinary people dislike AI, do not find it useful, do not want to live near datacenters, worry about jobs, and vote. One high-profile accident could make AI toxic.
A longer Macro Picture later this week will cover the fallout if the AI boom ends in a bust. It will not address whether AI is a bubble or when it might end.

sector_views.rationale: Perkins sees AI revenues as mostly capex recycling with returns well short of the hurdle rate, rising debt in the ecosystem, and cyclical hardware exposed to order cancellations and a shortage-to-glut swing. He does not issue a formal rating.

earnings_insights: Perkins says earnings disappointments in the AI ecosystem could cascade as cancelled orders, and this is the main channel through which AI debt becomes a problem.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Revenue needed to earn a decent return on AI capital, per studies cited since June. Against $200bn of enterprise revenue now, it implies a very large required increase.
The report gives this as the current level, with no reference period, and it is far below the hurdle rate.
Projected level of AI-related debt. Perkins says it is not systemic but is a risk if earnings disappoint.

risk_factors: AI revenue is mostly capex recycling rather than external demand.
Revenue falls well short of the $2.5-3.5 trillion a year needed by 2030.
Rapidly rising leverage at neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers and equipment/power providers, with AI debt possibly reaching $2 trillion by end-2027.
Cancelled orders cascading through the ecosystem if earnings disappoint, and chip order double-counting turning shortages into a glut.
Accounting practices flattering balance sheets, including the depreciation cliff and data center leases.
Hyperscalers may not renew all rolling datacenter leases.
External triggers: rate hikes, and a political backlash against AI and datacenters, including a high-profile accident.
vol_and_positioning: Perkins cites reports of companies double- and triple-ordering chips in anticipation of shortages, which creates bullwhip risk if demand slows.

tension_points.bull_case: AI bulls say revenues across the ecosystem are rising rapidly and compute demand is off the scale.
tension_points.bear_case: Perkins says the revenue is mostly capex recycling, and returns fall well short of the $2.5-3.5 trillion a year hurdle rate by 2030 against $200bn of enterprise revenue now.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Revenue shown to come mainly from businesses and end-users outside the ecosystem, paying for productivity-enhancing tools, would undercut the bear case.
